summary: We created Lunar Shark, an intuitive app built to help educators, mission planners and the curious evaluate and compare potential landing spots near the moon’s south pole. Instead of juggling complex tools, users can explore preset locations, drop custom coordinates, and pick exact mission dates. The platform pairs an interactive lunar map with dedicated sky views, giving a clear picture of how the Sun and Earth align with the local horizon. Planners can track these lighting and visibility shifts across a full timeline, animate changes to spot patterns instantly, and export datas for deeper study. By bringing mapping, astronomy, and timeline analysis together under one app, our project makes assessing solar illumination and communication links fast and friction free. With two flexible modes, it easily adapts to everyone from casual explorers to seasoned mission planners.
details:
Lunar Sharks is a 3D web tool for comparing lunar landing sites, custom coordinates and dates rapidly. By combining different resources from NASA's JPL Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, Lunaserv, LOLA South elevation models our project gives real representations of the moon and combining it with JPL Horizons data the program gives opportunity for planners to compare and understand landing sites with real visualisation. Moreover, we use LROC “Anthropogenic Features on the Moon” catalogue, in NASA’s PDS archive to represent old and latest landing sites.

How it works

When a user selects a site, Lunar Sharks shows what a lander standing there would actually see. For every site (custom sites too) we computed a 360° horizon from NASA elevation data. The program then checks hour by hour whether the Sun and Earth rise above that real horizon. From this it shows:

  • Sun and Earth status: each one’s angle above the level horizon, and whether the terrain blocks it (with the terrain’s height in that direction). For Earth it also shows its phase (how much of its disc is lit) and its apparent size in the sky.
  • Sun height: the Sun’s angle above the level horizon. At the south pole it stays within a few degrees, so even small hills can block it.
  • Solar flux now: the sunlight power reaching a panel facing the Sun, in W/m², based on how much of the Sun’s disc is above the terrain.
  • Sunrise/sunset and Earthrise/Earthset countdowns: when the Sun or Earth next appears or disappears behind the terrain, and how long it stays.
  • Sun visible and Earth visible: the share of time each is above the terrain.
  • Longest night: the longest stretch without sunlight, which the lander must survive on batteries.
  • Longest comms gap: the longest stretch without direct contact with Earth.
  • Peak and average Sun height: how high the Sun gets, and how high it is on average.
  • Average solar flux and solar energy: average sunlight on the panel and the total energy per square metre over the window.
  • Verdict: Strong, Mixed or Challenging, based on how often the Sun and Earth are both up.

Users choose mission dates anywhere from 2020 to 2050 and a shorter window to study, such as the first week after landing.Comparing sites “Compare all sites” ranks every site, custom sites included, for the chosen dates, shows a calendar of good and bad days, finds the best landing dates, and lets planners up to four date scenarios side by side.

Benefits and impact

Near the lunar south pole, the Sun skims only a degree or two above the horizon, so a single ridge can leave a lander in darkness for days. Thus, our project help mission planners, students and the public a free, fast way to understand why landing site and timing matter so much.

Tools

  • Javascript
  • three.js (WebGL) for 3D moon
  • Python
  • Netlify for hosting
  • Claude: SI was only used for explanations and for debugging the code. No photos of NASA was uploaded or generated. All the research was done by our team.

What makes it creative

Most lunar maps show the Moon from above. Lunar Sharks shows it from the lander’s point of view: a live horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth drawn to scale against the real terrain, showing even when only part of the Sun peeks over a ridge.

At the south pole, the surface uses real lighting: terrain shading driven by the Sun’s true position on the chosen date, so users can watch light and darkness sweep across the craters over a lunar day.

Users aren’t limited to our list. They can add any spot on the Moon by typing coordinates or clicking the globe, and the app computes its real horizon right in the browser from NASA elevation data.

Planning tools usually answer one question at a time. Lunar Sharks lets planners shift a whole mission by a lunar day with one click, compare up to four launch-delay scenarios, and find the best dates automatically.

Sun lighting switch. A Sun lighting switch (in Settings) flips between real lighting and the plain imagery.

Technical accuracy. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, including libration. Without an atmosphere, no refraction is applied, so the horizon is set only by the terrain and the curvature of the Moon. Horizons use the sharpest NASA elevation map available at each latitude.

One tool serves both experts and beginners, through Simple, Planner and Learn modes.

What factors did our team consider?

Site selection and comparison. Users can choose from past Apollo, Luna and Surveyor landings, Chinese, Indian and Japanese landers, and recent commercial missions (IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost 1). Positions come from the LROC catalogue, accurate to about 12 m. The south pole sites are NASA’s Artemis III candidate regions. Any custom coordinates can be added by typing or by clicking the Moon, and “Compare all sites” ranks every site side by side for the same dates.

Date and time flexibility. Mission dates can be anywhere from 2020 to 2050. Up to four date slip scenarios to compare launch delays. A calendar of good and bad days shows how conditions change across lunar days and seasons.

Sun and Earth visualization. A horizon panorama shows the Sun and Earth to scale against the real terrain. Countdowns show the time remaining until sunset and Earthset, the moments the challenge highlights as critical for operations.

Power and communication. Solar elevation is the most prominent number in the panel. Alongside it: solar flux and total energy, sunlight share, the longest night, Earth visibility, the longest communication gap, and lists of communication windows.

Multiple visualizations and temporal dynamics. A 3D globe built from LROC imagery, the 2D horizon panorama, a timeline of the whole mission, and a Play animation that shows the Sun and Earth moving over a lunar day.

Accessibility across skill levels. Simple mode for the public, Planner mode with full detail and CSV export for engineers, a Learn section explaining why the Moon is so hard to plan for, and a step-by-step guide.
